question: Can invariant imbedding turn continuous-depth neural-network training from a forward-then-backward boundary-value calculation into depth-indexed initial-value systems whose intermediate depths are directly observable and whose gradients need no preceding forward solve?

key_findings.claim: The soundest part of the construction is a depth-sensitivity identity for a consistently restricted ODE flow.
key_findings.evidence: Writing the trajectory as z(t;p,x), Theorem 1 relates moving the input location p to perturbing x through partial_p z = -partial_x z f(p,x,theta(p)). This is the flow/semigroup identity behind invariant imbedding and permits endpoint outputs z(q;p,x) for a family of start depths to be advanced from the trivial state z(q;q,x)=x.

key_findings.claim: A decisive proof gap invalidates the stated derivation of the invariant-imbedding identity for the adjoint under the paper's assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix E.5 prints Equation 53 as only the expression [partial_theta f]^T(partial_p lambda + partial_x lambda f), without an equality. Even if '=0' is supplied as the evident intended statement, the authors infer the parenthesized vector is zero merely because partial_theta f is 'not identically 0.' A nonzero matrix can have a nontrivial nullspace; injectivity or an appropriate full-rank condition is required. Equation 54 is then used throughout the derivation of Theorem 2, so the advertised general backward initial-value system and downstream optimality derivation are not established as written.

anchors.section: Appendix E.7 / derivation of Theorems 2 and 3

key_findings.claim: The claimed general solution also assumes an unproved horizon-consistency relation for the control.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 begins with a fixed admissible control theta(t), for which the trajectory flow identity is natural. The text then permits theta(t;p,x) to depend on input and starting depth and asserts partial_p theta = -partial_x theta f 'by the same' invariant-imbedding relation, although theta has no state evolution law and independently optimized controls on different horizons need not be restrictions of one common control. Appendix E.4 dispatches this step with 'mutatis mutandis.' That extra compatibility must be assumed or proved before the adjoint construction can represent a general nonlinear vector-valued Bolza problem.

key_findings.claim: The benchmark experiments do not test the paper's headline forward-pass-independent training method.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4 states that every benchmark except projectile motion differentiates through the discrete system using ordinary backpropagation. The released rotating-MNIST and bouncing-balls notebooks likewise optimize TensorFlow gradient-tape losses through their forward computations. Theorem 2's imbedded-adjoint update is used only in the four-sample projectile experiment, which the authors say performs poorly because exact nested Jacobians exhaust RAM at higher resolution.

key_findings.claim: The practical architecture replaces the exact depth dynamics with an uncontrolled Jacobian approximation.
key_findings.evidence: Exact evaluation would accumulate higher-order input derivatives with depth. Equation 21 drops the higher-order terms and approximates the Jacobian recurrence using partial_x Phi. No truncation-error bound, stability condition, exact-versus-approximate ablation, gradient check, or scaling study is reported. The appendix explicitly says the exact computation grows exponentially with depth, making the approximation central rather than incidental to the benchmark results.

anchors.section: 3.2 Numerical approximation of input gradients / Equations 16--21

key_findings.claim: Rotating-MNIST results are competitive with the selected baselines, but the evidence does not establish a superior or more efficient training method overall.
key_findings.evidence: Across two- and three-layer Phi networks and depths one through four, InImNet reports held-out-frame MSE 0.0125--0.0176; the best imported comparator is 0.0122 with a very large stated standard deviation of 0.0064. Per-epoch InImNet times are 3.15--5.85 seconds versus 8.636 seconds for that comparator. The comparison imports baseline outcomes, reports no parameter counts, memory, total convergence time, function evaluations, timing variance, or accuracy-matched stopping, and only InImNet receives a ten-seed study under the authors' implementation.

key_findings.claim: The main bouncing-balls model is faster per epoch than one reimplemented comparator but materially less accurate than the strongest plotted baselines.
key_findings.evidence: The depth-three MLP InImNet reaches MSE 0.0192 in 153 seconds per epoch versus Vialard et al.'s 0.0146 in 516 seconds, making its error about 31.5% higher. Figure 4 also plots ODE2VAE at 0.0093, about half the InImNet error, but the adjacent table omits it. The timing covers one public-Colab configuration against only Vialard, with no repetitions, hardware identity, variance, memory, parameter count, total runtime, or common stopping criterion.

key_findings.claim: The convolutional bouncing-balls extension improves on the cited shooting model but still lacks a controlled state-of-the-art comparison.
key_findings.evidence: At depth three the convolutional variant reports MSE 0.0122 versus 0.0146 for Vialard et al., but the 0.0093 ODE2VAE result plotted in the same figure remains lower. Figure 8's caption says its right panel contains average time per epoch, while that panel actually contains only MSE values and no convolutional timing. Results have no seed variation or error bars.

key_findings.claim: Outputs at unoptimized depths expose failure trajectories, but they are not generally valid predictions or an established explainability method.
key_findings.evidence: Depth extrapolation requires a different tied-Phi architecture because the principal model has independent parameters at each layer. That tied variant performs worse on rotating MNIST; deeper samples lose diversity. On bouncing balls, it erases the sequence and later reverses it, which the authors interpret as revealing what the network learned. These are qualitative degradation traces, not validated explanations, and contradict the conclusion's broader wording that each layer depicts a valid output.

anchors.section: 4.2 Extrapolation beyond optimised models and conclusion

key_findings.claim: The projectile-motion result demonstrates an executable adjoint path but not successful time-series prediction.
key_findings.evidence: The demonstration uses four samples, five p positions, ten epochs, and exact automatic-differentiation Jacobians. The authors explicitly report that this is the maximum resolution before RAM exhaustion and that performance is poor for lack of resolution and data. It is therefore a minimal implementation check for the specialized endpoint-observation formulation, not empirical support for competitive time-series learning.

key_findings.claim: The released artifact is informative source code but does not reproduce the reported experiments without substantial reconstruction.
key_findings.evidence: The repository provides seven notebooks, a TensorFlow script, a developmental PyTorch package, and rendered figures, but no datasets, downloader, dependency/environment lock, setup metadata, checkpoints, raw benchmark logs, license, CI, or executed outputs for the training notebooks. Most notebooks mount an author's Google Drive and require unshipped paths. README links name two absent notebooks. More importantly, the paper specifies 100 epochs for MLP bouncing balls and 20 for the convolutional run, whereas the released notebooks set 500 for both; the artifact cannot identify which settings generated the paper figures.

method.core_idea: Make the starting depth p and invariant input x explicit, then evolve endpoint outputs and adjoint quantities across p rather than solving each network forward in trajectory time t and then backward in t.
method.mechanism: A flow sensitivity PDE advances z(q;p,x) from z(q;q,x)=x. The paper proposes a companion p-indexed adjoint Lambda(p,x), an endpoint stationarity condition for the control, Euler discretizations over depth, and numerical or truncated approximations to the nested input Jacobians. Experiments embed autoencoder latents in layer-specific or tied MLP/convolutional Phi maps and train almost all variants with conventional backpropagation.
assumptions: The ODE dynamics are sufficiently regular and solutions exist uniquely over every embedded interval
Controls on different starting depths and inputs are restrictions of a horizon-consistent family
The control Jacobian has enough rank to infer the adjoint invariant-imbedding relation, although the stated theorem assumes only nontrivial dependence
A first-order stationarity condition meaningfully characterizes the desired optimal control
Nested input derivatives can be evaluated or approximated stably as depth and dimension grow
Dropping higher-order terms in the Jacobian recurrence preserves useful optimization directions
Imported benchmark values use sufficiently matched data, preprocessing, model capacity, and selection protocols
Per-epoch wall time on a public Colab configuration is a meaningful efficiency proxy

techniques.role: Evolves endpoint predictions across nested start intervals using a p-indexed flow-sensitivity equation.
Attempts to propagate loss derivatives from the trivial network across depth without first solving a trajectory forward.
Links the endpoint control Psi and dynamics Phi to an optimal-control first-order condition.
Drops higher-order input-gradient terms to make the discrete benchmarks computationally feasible.
Ties Phi across layers so the trained dynamics can be inspected before and beyond the optimized depth.
Uses running-loss impulses to learn a family of trajectories from endpoints observed at different starting positions.

evaluations.setting: Rotating MNIST with one input frame, sixteen target angles, selected held-out frames, ten random initializations, two- or three-layer Phi MLPs, and depths one through four
evaluations.metric: held-out fifth-frame MSE and seconds per epoch
evaluations.result: InImNet MSE 0.0125--0.0176 and 3.15--5.85 seconds per epoch
evaluations.baseline: imported GPPVAE/ODE2VAE values and Vialard et al. at 0.0122 +/- 0.0064 and 8.636 seconds per epoch

evaluations.setting: Bouncing balls with autoencoder latent, three-layer Phi MLP, and depths one through three
evaluations.metric: sequence MSE and seconds per epoch
evaluations.result: MSE improves from 0.0234 to 0.0192 while time grows from 91 to 153 seconds per epoch
evaluations.baseline: Vialard et al. 0.0146 and 516 seconds per epoch; plotted ODE2VAE 0.0093 with no timing comparison

evaluations.setting: Convolutional bouncing-balls InImNet at depths one through three
evaluations.baseline: Vialard et al. 0.0146 and plotted ODE2VAE 0.0093; no timing or seed uncertainty

evaluations.setting: Tied-Phi depth extrapolation on rotating MNIST and bouncing balls
evaluations.metric: per-frame MSE curves and qualitative generated sequences across p=0 to p=-8
evaluations.result: rotating-digit quality and diversity degrade away from trained p=-4; bouncing-ball predictions erase and then reverse beyond trained p=-3
evaluations.baseline: the untied benchmark architecture cannot extrapolate because each layer has separate Phi parameters

evaluations.setting: Projectile trajectories learned from endpoints at four start positions plus the terminal point
evaluations.metric: qualitative endpoint fit after ten epochs
evaluations.result: authors report poor performance but successful execution of the imbedded-adjoint update
evaluations.baseline: none; four samples and five p positions are the maximum reported before RAM exhaustion

limitations: Author-stated: nested Jacobian computation grows prohibitively with depth and dimension; exact time-series training exhausted available RAM at five p positions.
Author-stated: the experiments do not explore Theorem 3's depth-optimality implications.
Author-stated: extrapolation with tied dynamics performs worse and can erase or reverse bouncing-ball sequences.
Reviewer audit: the adjoint proof makes an invalid nonzero-matrix-to-injectivity inference, so the principal general theorem is not established under its stated assumptions.
Reviewer audit: horizon consistency of input- and depth-dependent optimal controls is asserted rather than proved.
Reviewer audit: the benchmark evidence concerns an approximate discrete architecture trained by standard backpropagation, not the headline independent backward solver.
Reviewer audit: comparisons omit parameter count, memory, function evaluations, total convergence time, matched stopping, repeated timing, and several stronger plotted baselines.
Reviewer audit: only small synthetic video tasks and an admitted unsuccessful four-sample regression demonstration are evaluated.
Reviewer audit: source and repository settings disagree, and the unshipped data and environments prevent exact reproduction.
failure_modes: A rank-deficient control Jacobian leaves adjoint components unconstrained, breaking the step from Equation 53 to Equation 54.
Controls optimized separately for different horizons need not compose under the asserted invariant-imbedding rule.
Nested input derivatives can exhaust memory or amplify perturbations exponentially with depth.
Cropping higher-order Jacobian terms can introduce unmeasured bias or instability into the learned depth dynamics.
Per-epoch speed can hide slower convergence, different parameter counts, weaker terminal accuracy, or higher preprocessing cost.
Tying dynamics to enable extrapolation can reduce fit quality and collapse sequence diversity.
Intermediate-depth outputs can be visually interpretable but invalid, degenerate, or time-reversed predictions.
Notebook dependence on private Drive paths, absent datasets, and mismatched epochs can silently produce results different from the paper.
Solver and discretization error can dominate any continuous-depth interpretation when only a coarse Euler scheme is tested.
reusable_insights: Treat the network start location as an explicit variable when a family of nested horizons is itself the object of study.
Separate a flow-sensitivity identity, an optimal-control condition, and a practical training algorithm; validity of one does not validate the others.
Before cancelling a Jacobian in a proof, state and verify the exact injectivity or rank condition required.
Benchmark novel gradient methods by checking their gradients against autodiff and by training the headline experiments with the claimed gradient path.
Report approximation error as depth grows, not only terminal task error, when higher-order derivatives are deliberately truncated.
Depth traces are useful failure diagnostics even when they are not faithful explanations or valid predictions.
Efficiency comparisons should match error, hardware, parameter count, memory, stopping rule, and total training time rather than one epoch alone.
Archive exact datasets, executable environments, seeds, raw logs, and paper-matched configurations when notebooks expose several divergent settings.
open_questions: Can the adjoint theorem be repaired with explicit full-rank conditions, or can a different derivation avoid cancelling the control Jacobian?
What compatibility conditions guarantee that optimal controls across varying start depths form an invariantly embedded family?
Does the independent imbedded-adjoint algorithm produce gradients matching conventional adjoints on controlled nonlinear vector Bolza problems?
How does Jacobian-cropping error scale with depth, width, step size, and Lyapunov spectrum?
Can Jacobian-vector products, reversible solvers, checkpointing, or implicit differentiation retain exactness at lower cost than the proposed truncation?
Does any InImNet variant beat modern Neural-ODE solvers or adaptive-depth ResNets under accuracy-, compute-, and memory-matched conditions?
Can intermediate-depth outputs be evaluated for calibrated validity rather than visual plausibility?
Which paper results, if any, are reproduced by the released 500-epoch notebook settings rather than the 20- or 100-epoch manuscript settings?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.relationship: foundational continuous-depth model and adjoint baseline
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. parameterize hidden-state derivatives and use black-box ODE solvers plus an adjoint sensitivity method. InImNet instead indexes endpoint maps by their starting depth and proposes an adjoint initial-value system over that depth, but its benchmark notebooks retain conventional backpropagation and a coarse Euler discretization.

competitive_landscape.title: ANODE: Unconditionally Accurate Memory-Efficient Gradients for Neural ODEs
competitive_landscape.difference: ANODE identifies numerical instability and optimize-then-discretize inconsistency in the original adjoint and combines checkpointing with exact discrete gradients. It addresses the same memory motivation without InImNet's unvalidated adjoint-cancellation step or deliberate higher-order Jacobian truncation.

competitive_landscape.title: Augmented Neural ODEs
competitive_landscape.difference: Dupont et al. prove topological expressivity limits of ordinary Neural ODEs and add dimensions to improve expressivity, stability, and cost. InImNet mentions compatibility with augmentation but neither incorporates it nor tests whether its depth embedding changes those expressivity limits.

competitive_landscape.title: A Shooting Formulation of Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest optimal-control architecture baseline used by the target
competitive_landscape.difference: Vialard et al. parameterize optimal continuous-depth weight trajectories through initial conditions and particle ensembles. InImNet imports its rotating-MNIST and bouncing-balls protocols, replaces trajectory-time shooting with start-depth imbedding, and is faster per reported epoch but usually less accurate in the main experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: Depth-Adaptive Neural Networks from the Optimal Control viewpoint
competitive_landscape.difference: Cipriani et al. progressively refine the time discretization and prove convergence to an underlying continuous problem when tolerances hold. This provides an operational depth-adaptation procedure, whereas InImNet exposes p and suggests optimizing it but explicitly leaves Theorem 3's depth optimization unexplored.

competitive_landscape.title: MALI: A memory efficient and reverse accurate integrator for Neural ODEs
competitive_landscape.difference: MALI uses a reversible asynchronous-leapfrog integrator to obtain constant solver-step memory while preserving reverse-trajectory and gradient accuracy, including ImageNet-scale evidence. It targets the central efficiency problem more directly and at much larger scale than InImNet's approximate-Jacobian synthetic benchmarks.

competitive_landscape.title: Interplay between depth and width for interpolation in neural ODEs
competitive_landscape.relationship: current theory of continuous-depth architecture requirements
competitive_landscape.difference: Álvarez-López et al. derive quantitative depth-width tradeoffs for finite-dataset and measure interpolation. Their results formalize architecture capacity, whereas InImNet's claim that explicit p illuminates depth is supported only by qualitative loss and output traces.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive higher order reversible integrators for memory efficient deep learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: current variable-step and memory-efficient continuous-depth competitor
competitive_landscape.difference: Maslovskaya et al. develop adaptive higher-order reversible integration so training memory is independent of depth while irregular time points and numerical accuracy remain controllable. This contrasts with InImNet's first-order Euler method and unbounded nested-Jacobian burden.

competitive_landscape.title: An optimal control approach for neural network architecture adaptation with a posteriori error estimation
competitive_landscape.relationship: current primary work on principled depth adaptation
competitive_landscape.difference: Meisrimel and Ulbrich derive a posteriori error estimates that localize discretization error and drive insertion of layers where estimated error is largest. This turns continuous optimal-control theory into an error-controlled architecture-adaptation rule, a stronger realization of depth inspection than InImNet's uncalibrated extrapolation curves.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Invariant imbedding yields a general solution for nonlinear vector-valued Bolza control problems, enables independent forward and backward depth evolution, exposes neural-network depth as an optimizable variable, and produces competitive, efficient continuous-depth architectures.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper states three theorems, derives a depth-indexed endpoint equation, an imbedded adjoint and stationarity condition, presents one algorithm, and reports rotating-MNIST, bouncing-balls, depth-extrapolation, convolutional, and projectile demonstrations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Applying invariant imbedding to a family of neural endpoint maps is a distinctive conceptual contribution, and Theorem 1's flow-sensitivity view is potentially reusable. The stronger novelty claims are not sustained: the adjoint proof cancels a merely nonzero matrix without the needed rank condition, control-family consistency is assumed, headline benchmarks use ordinary backpropagation and an uncontrolled derivative approximation, and efficiency evidence is partial. The work should be treated as an interesting but mathematically incomplete and experimentally preliminary formulation, not a validated general replacement for Neural-ODE adjoints or a state-of-the-art depth optimizer.

reviewer_notes: Read the exact 22-page pinned primary PDF end to end, including all 59 numbered displayed equations, three theorems, Algorithm 1, nine numbered figures, four numbered tables, and Appendices A--G. A freshly downloaded official arXiv PDF was byte-identical to the cache (SHA-256 1ae3439164e644ff65be7fea8a452bb97d0302090ac7c3298fc7033de2c088be). The current v2 source bundle was inspected in full, including TeX, bibliography, every rendered figure asset, rotating-MNIST timing logs, and its one timing-calculation script. The official linked GitHub repository was audited at current main commit 6b20d0743c4390682858d1738ef2bce8c7e3e041 (2022-02-14): it contains the experimental notebooks and developmental PyTorch code but no license, datasets, environment lock, package metadata, raw training logs, checkpoints, CI, or executed training outputs. Six of seven training notebooks have no executed cells. Notebook data paths depend on an author's Google Drive or absent local datasets; two README notebook links are stale. Paper/repository epoch mismatches were checked directly: the MLP bouncing-balls notebook sets 500 versus 100 in Table 3, and the convolutional notebook sets 500 versus 20 in Table 4. Equation 53 was checked against both rendered PDF and TeX: it has no equality, and the subsequent inference would remain invalid even if '=0' were restored because nonzero does not imply injective. OpenReview's automated routes were challenge-blocked, so the collection's documented exact-title arXiv source override was used without changing the OpenReview identity. Competitor titles, abstracts, and relationships were checked against current primary arXiv records through 2026-08-24.
